title.en: Time of day as a sun arc: elevation, colour and shadow length

summary: Pick one sun elevation and azimuth for the hour you want, then read key colour, intensity and shadow length off a single table so every light in the scene agrees with that one direction.
objective: The stated hour is legible without a caption: shadow length matches the sun elevation, the shaded side carries the complementary sky colour, and no second light contradicts the declared direction.
intent_signals: what sun position for this time of day
make the shadows the right length for noon
animate the sun across the day
example_prompts: Set the terrain scene at 9am and get the shadow length right.
Move a street scene from noon to blue hour in one pass.
Choose a sun elevation that makes the roof forms read.
negative_signals: real solar position for a given date and latitude
interior scene lit only by fixtures
not_for: Astronomical or engineering solar position, which requires a sourced solar model with date, latitude and longitude.
Solar gain, irradiance or daylight-factor analysis, which needs measured units rather than authored intensities.

principles: Elevation is the whole story of the hour. Shadow length is the cotangent of the elevation, so 5 deg gives shadows about eleven times the caster height, 25 deg about two, and 60 deg about half: the number the viewer reads first.
Colour follows elevation because low sun travels through more atmosphere. Warm key against a blue fill at the ends of the day, near-neutral key against a pale fill in the middle.
Azimuth is a composition choice, not a physical one here. Put the sun off the camera axis so shadows run across the frame and describe the ground.
After sunset the key is gone but the sky is not: blue hour is a bright hemispheric fill with no cast shadow, and treating it as a dim sun produces the usual wrong-looking dusk.
Every value in the table is relative to a stated tone mapping and exposure; copying an intensity into a different exposure changes the hour it reads as.
implementation: Choose the hour, then take elevation, key colour, key intensity and fill from the sun_arc table and set the DirectionalLight from spherical coordinates once.
Set the hemisphere fill sky colour to the complement of the key: cool blue for warm low sun, pale neutral for high sun, and a saturated blue at civil dusk.
Fit the shadow camera to the visible extent and expect a longer extent at low elevations, because the shadows themselves are long.
Verify the shadow-length ratio against the table with a single vertical test post before dressing the scene.
To animate the day, interpolate elevation and azimuth along the arc and drive colour and intensity from the same parameter, so the three never disagree.
At dusk (elevation below 0 deg) turn castShadow off on the key or remove the key entirely and raise the hemisphere fill; keep a warm horizon band in the sky gradient.
State the tone mapping and exposure alongside the chosen row; these values assume ACESFilmic at exposure 1.0.
observable_checks: A one-metre vertical post casts a shadow whose length matches the table row within about ten percent.
All shadows in the frame run parallel and agree with the single declared azimuth.
The shaded side of a neutral object samples cool and non-zero at low sun, and near-neutral at midday.
At the dusk row there is no cast shadow anywhere, and the scene still separates ground from sky.
A grayscale screenshot still reads the hour from shadow length alone.

creative_affordances: Colours can be pushed far past any real sky as long as the shadow length and the single sun direction still agree with the stated hour.
The arc can be compressed, reversed or given an invented second sun; the table is a starting geometry, not a calendar.
known_limits: Authored creative table, not a solar model: no date, latitude, longitude, atmospheric turbidity or measured irradiance is represented, and the Kelvin-to-hex colours are authored approximations rather than colorimetric transforms.
Intensities were tuned for ACESFilmic tone mapping at exposure 1.0 and must be re-derived under any other curve or exposure.
No renderer was run for this record: the shadow-length ratios are trigonometric, while the colours and intensities are authored.

defaults.rationale: Rows are spaced so each reads as a distinct hour rather than a slider position: 5, 25, 60, 35, 8 and -2 deg elevation give shadow ratios of about 11.4, 2.1, 0.6, 1.4, 7.1 and none. The ratios are cot(elevation) and are exact; the colours and intensities are authored for ACESFilmic at exposure 1.0 and are the part to retune first.

dawn.note: pale key, cool ambient, mist sits low

noon.note: flattest hour; form has to come from material and fill

golden_hour.note: see knowledge.lighting-mood-dusk-golden-hour for the full rig

dusk_civil.note: blue hour: hemisphere fill only, no cast shadow, warm horizon band

values.shadow_length_rule: length / caster height = cot(elevation); check with one vertical post before dressing the scene
values.azimuth_rule: keep the sun 30-70 deg off the camera axis so shadows cross the frame
never: a second light that casts shadows in a different direction
a dim sun standing in for blue hour
claiming a real solar position for a date and latitude
